articles.title: Smoking just 1 cigarette a day: Is there a safe number for your heart?
articles.summary: One cigarette after lunch. Another with a cup of tea. Maybe one more at the end of a stressful day.
articles.body: One cigarette after lunch. Another with a cup of tea. Maybe one more at the end of a stressful day. For someone who smokes just a few cigarettes, the habit may not feel like a serious threat to the heart. After all, it is not a full pack a day.But the heart does not measure cigarette smoke in neat little portions. Even one cigarette a day can carry a surprisingly large share of the cardiovascular risk linked to heavier smoking. And the damage is not limited to the lungs. The chemicals inhaled with every puff can affect blood vessels, circulation and the way blood clots.So, is there a number of cigarettes you can smoke every day without putting your heart at risk? Doctors say there is no established safe limit. Cutting down may reduce exposure to harmful substances, but it does not remove the cardiovascular risks of smoking.This World Heart Day, the question is worth asking: what exactly happens inside the body when someone believes they are smoking too little to cause harm?“There is a common belief among the public that smoking only a few cigarettes every day is harmless compared to smoking heavily. Unfortunately, there is no agreed safety limit of smoking in terms of heart health. Even small amounts of smoking lead to taking nicotine, carbon monoxide and other toxic substances into the body, which create problems for blood vessels and the heart itself,” Dr Sameer Gupta, Sr Interventional Cardiologist, Group Head - Cath Labs, Director - Metro Group of Hospitals told Times of India.Dr Gupta explains that smoking affects the walls of blood vessels, inflaming them and making the blood more prone to clotting. Nicotine affects heart rate and blood pressure. Over time, these changes can contribute to atherosclerosis, a condition in which plaque builds up inside the arteries.The surprising part: One cigarette a day can carry a large share of the riskA large 2018 analysis published in the British Medical Journal looked at data from 141 cohort studies examining smoking and the risk of coronary heart disease and stroke.The researchers found that smoking about one cigarette a day was associated with roughly 40–50% of the excess risk of coronary heart disease and stroke seen in people who smoked 20 cigarettes a day. In other words, the cardiovascular risk did not fall in direct proportion to the number of cigarettes smoked.The analysis found that smoking one cigarette a day was associated with a 48% higher risk of coronary heart disease in men and a 57% higher risk in women in the primary estimates.That is what makes light smoking so easy to underestimate. Someone who has cut down from a pack a day to just one or two cigarettes may feel they have reduced their risk by a similar amount. But cardiovascular risk does not decline in a simple, straight line as cigarette consumption falls. The BMJ analysis concluded that even low levels of smoking are associated with a substantial risk of heart disease and stroke, and that quitting completely is the most effective way to reduce that risk.Occasional smoking can quietly become a daily habitFor some people, smoking is tied to a particular moment rather than a fixed daily routine. It may happen at a party, during a stressful day or when meeting friends. That can create the impression that occasional smoking is too infrequent to matter.But Dr Akshat Malik, Senior Consultant, Head & Neck Oncology, Apollo Hospitals, Delhi, says there is no established safe amount of cigarettes that can be smoked without adversely affecting the heart. He points out that even low levels of smoking can harm cardiovascular health.“Smoking only one cigarette per day may have far more serious cardiovascular implications than many people believe. Reducing the number of times one smokes can decrease exposure to the toxins found in cigarettes, but it does not mean the person is safe because he still smokes. The safest option in terms of protection for the heart is to abstain from smoking altogether,” says Dr Malik.Nicotine is highly addictive, and a cigarette linked to a particular situation can gradually become a regular part of the day. The occasional cigarette may become a daily one, especially when smoking is used to cope with stress or social pressure.Dr Malik cautions that the idea of smoking just one cigarette during social events or stressful moments can create a false sense of control over the habit. The concern is not only that occasional smoking may become more frequent. Even when it remains occasional, exposure to tobacco smoke is not considered safe for the heart.How quickly does the heart begin to benefit after quitting?The health benefits of quitting smoking begin sooner than many people expect. According to the WHO, heart rate and blood pressure begin to fall within about 20 minutes of quitting. Within 12 hours, carbon monoxide levels in the blood return to normal. Over the following weeks, circulation and lung function improve.After about a year without smoking, the risk of coronary heart disease is roughly half that of someone who continues to smoke. Over the longer term, the risk continues to decline. These timelines are general estimates. Recovery varies depending on a person’s smoking history, overall health and other risk factors. But the message is clear: quitting can make a meaningful difference, even for people who have smoked for years.World Heart Day: The heart risk that can hide in plain sightObserved every year on September 29, World Heart Day raises awareness about cardiovascular disease and the steps people can take to protect their heart health.The World Heart Federation’s 2026 campaign carries the message “Don’t miss a beat.” It highlights the need to recognise cardiovascular risks and take action before they lead to serious complications.Smoking is one such risk. It can damage blood vessels and raise the risk of heart disease even when the number of cigarettes smoked each day seems small. And the risk does not stop with the person holding the cigarette. Second-hand smoke can also harm the cardiovascular health of people nearby. The WHO says there is no safe level of exposure to second-hand tobacco smoke.For people who smoke, the next step does not have to be taken alone. A doctor can help identify suitable quitting methods, including counselling and nicotine replacement therapy, and help manage withdrawal symptoms and cravings.This World Heart Day, the takeaway is simple: when it comes to protecting your heart, there is no safe cigarette count. The goal is not to find a number you can get away with, but to stop smoking altogether.

articles.title: Delhi-NCR children with asthma, allergies at risk as weather patterns change
articles.summary: With changing weather conditions across Delhi‑NCR, experts are witnessing increased concerns related to asthma, allergic rhinitis, recurrent cough,
articles.body: With changing weather conditions across Delhi‑NCR, experts are witnessing increased concerns related to asthma, allergic rhinitis, recurrent cough, wheezing and other respiratory symptoms among children. Sudden changes in temperature, increased humidity, dust, air pollution and exposure to seasonal allergens can irritate the airways and trigger symptoms, particularly in children who already have asthma or allergies.Experts say that while weather changes do not cause asthma or allergies on their own, they can act as important triggers and make existing symptoms worse.“Children with asthma and allergies often have sensitive airways, and sudden changes in weather can make them more reactive. We commonly see children developing increased coughing, wheezing, chest tightness, sneezing, a blocked or runny nose and breathing discomfort when there is a sudden change in temperature or humidity. Exposure to dust, pollen, smoke and air pollution can further aggravate these symptoms. Parents should therefore pay attention to changes in their child’s breathing pattern and not dismiss a persistent cough or repeated wheezing as just a seasonal infection. Children who have already been diagnosed with asthma should continue their prescribed treatment and follow their asthma action plan, particularly during periods when known triggers are high,” said Dr Manish Balde, senior paediatrician, Motherhood Hospital, Gurgaon.“Weather changes can affect children differently depending on their underlying health. Cold air may irritate sensitive airways, while humidity and sudden temperature fluctuations can create conditions that worsen respiratory discomfort. At the same time, Delhi‑NCR’s air pollution and high levels of dust can add another layer of irritation. Children who have allergic rhinitis may experience increased sneezing, nasal congestion, itchy or watery eyes, and a runny nose, while those with asthma may develop coughing, wheezing, or difficulty breathing. Parents should understand that not every cough or breathing problem is asthma, but recurring symptoms deserve evaluation. If a child frequently coughs at night, develops wheezing during exercise, or gets breathless while playing, then consult a paediatrician. Keeping the child away from cigarette smoke, incense, strong fragrances, dust and other known irritants can help reduce exposure. During poor air‑quality days, outdoor activity may need to be limited, especially for children whose asthma is not well controlled,” the doctor added.Parents should not stop or change prescribed asthma medication simply because the child appears better. Asthma is a long‑term condition that can often be controlled effectively with the right treatment and monitoring. Children with allergies may also require appropriate treatment depending on their symptoms and triggers. Self‑medication, particularly with antibiotics or cough syrups, should be avoided unless recommended by a doctor.“Prevention is important in children with a known history of asthma or allergies. Parents can encourage regular hand hygiene, ensure adequate sleep and nutrition, reduce exposure to dust and smoke, and keep prescribed medicines readily available when advised. They should also know the warning signs that require urgent medical attention, such as severe breathing difficulty, difficulty speaking or eating because of breathlessness, bluish lips, extreme tiredness, or symptoms that are rapidly worsening. With timely medical care and good trigger control, most children with asthma and allergies can continue their normal school, play, and daily activities,” said Dr Manish Balde.

articles.title: Gaza doctors face tough decisions as patients face long waits for diagnoses
articles.summary: Medical staff in Gaza struggle to treat patients with shortages in testing equipment.
articles.body:
Deir el-Balah, Gaza – At Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital here in central Gaza, Bassem Hassan, director of the laboratory department, deals with medical tests whose results will determine the futures of his patients.

Hassan’s team gives doctors the information they need to diagnose a range of illnesses, from kidney disease to diabetes, and without this crucial information, they will not know how to proceed with their cases.

But Israel’s genocidal war and siege on Gaza has resulted in widespread damage to medical infrastructure and shortages of key materials needed to make diagnoses.

There has been a suspension of all blood gas testing, which is particularly important for cardiac and intensive-care patients, and shortages of blood-collection tubes, which are essential for clinical chemistry tests.

Automated clinical chemistry analysers, which laboratories rely on for more than 60 percent of their tests, have also stopped operating. Some sterilisation equipment and refrigerators used to store blood and plasma have also ceased working.

“Given these limited resources, tests are prioritised according to the severity of each case with priority given to kidney, cancer and heart patients as well as those in intensive care,” Hassan told Al Jazeera.

Doctors know that laboratory test results are needed to determine the correct medication dosages given to patients, monitor their responses to treatment and make urgent medical decisions.

Without this information, doctors are left without a key part of the jigsaw puzzle that could determine the death or survival of a patient.

As the third anniversary of the war on Gaza approaches, more than three-quarters of medical imaging equipment in the enclave is out of service. Shortages of laboratory testing materials are at 87 percent, and there is a 74 percent deficit in essential consumables required for laboratory and diagnostic testing.

Gaza’s ministry of health has warned that with these dire shortages and repeated breakdowns of medical equipment, blood banks and laboratories risk shutting down.

This would most affect patients suffering from critical conditions, such as electrolyte imbalances, high potassium levels, impaired kidney function and heart disease.

Marwan Al-Azaiza, head of the cardiology department at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital, told Al Jazeera that due to these shortages at public hospitals, doctors sometimes have to use private laboratories if the patients can afford this added expense.

“In other cases, doctors rely on clinical examinations, electrocardiograms and the indicators available to them, even though this does not constitute a complete substitute for the tests needed to confirm or rule out certain diagnoses,” he said.

Medical teams are looking to coordinate with charities, health organisations and relief institutions to provide broader care for the people of Gaza.

Meanwhile, only five of the 18 CT scanners in Gaza remain operational, and the remaining ones are running beyond their capacity.

There are also no magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) services in Gaza after the destruction of nine machines in Israeli attacks.

Mohammed Abu Salmiya, director of al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City, told Al Jazeera that medical teams are now forced to restrict laboratory tests, X-rays and CT scans to the most urgent cases.

“This reality forces doctors to make difficult choices between patients, deciding who needs the test immediately and whose test can be postponed,” he told Al Jazeera.

“Although this approach is necessary under the current shortages, it means that many other patients remain on waiting lists with diagnostic tests delayed even when they are needed to diagnose their conditions or monitor their treatment.”

Yousef al-Athamneh, 57, from Deir el-Balah suffers from kidney failure and requires dialysis three times a week. He worries about the shortages of bicarbonate, bloodlines, dialysis machines, intravenous fluids and other materials that are needed for his dialysis sessions.

“What frightens me most is the possibility that one day dialysis supplies will run out or that a machine will break down while replacement parts are unavailable, leaving me unable to access the treatment that keeps me alive,” he told Al Jazeera. “All we ask is for the most basic necessities of medical care to be available, so that we can go to our dialysis sessions with the reassurance that we will return home to our families.”

Khalil Al-Daqran, spokesperson for Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital, said cancer patients are facing shortages of chemotherapy drugs and other medicines. The destruction of the Turkish-Palestinian Friendship Hospital, the only hospital in Gaza that had specialised in cancer treatment, has also added to the strain on medical teams.

Israel’s tightened siege on Gaza means it is almost impossible for cancer patients to seek treatment abroad, Al-Daqran added.

Overall, 350,000 patients with chronic diseases, including diabetes and high blood pressure, face medication shortages, which pose a threat to the continuity of their treatment and their lives, he added.

“Cancer patients, people living with chronic illnesses and those suffering from heart and kidney disease require regular treatment that cannot be postponed while doctors are being forced to work with extremely limited resources,” Al-Daqran said.

“What we need now is guaranteed access to medicines, medical supplies and equipment, so that shortages do not become an additional cause of deaths that could have been prevented.”

articles.title: 282 vs. 233: Closing India's heart attack gap
articles.summary: I have opened more chests than I can count. In the early years of my career, the patient on my table was mostly sixty years and above.
articles.body: I have opened more chests than I can count. In the early years of my career, the patient on my table was mostly sixty years and above. As early as 2010s, this began to change. I still remember the case of 28 year old Vishnu Yadav, who had an aneurysm emerging from his left ventricle. I remember this very clearly because his aneurysm or swelling was five times as big as his heart.Today, I routinely operate on men and women in their early forties. Some are in their thirties and twenties. This is not a statistic to me; every patient is a life I care about. I feel the wound every time I make an incision.So let me put the numbers plainly. India's age-standardized cardiovascular death rate stands at 282 per 100,000 people. The global average is 233. We are not catching up to the world's heart health; for some reason, we are falling further behind, even as our hospitals fill with technology the world's best centers would envy and we speak ad nauseum about big data and AI.This is the paradox I want you to sit with. In our best urban hospitals, we now have AI algorithms that can flag a heart attack risk years before symptoms appear. We have genetic panels that map a patient's inherited vulnerabilities down to specific gene variants. We have new-generation lipid-lowering drugs ( PCSK9 inhibitors and beyond) that can drive LDL cholesterol to levels we once thought biologically impossible. If technology alone could save hearts, India's urban elite should be the healthiest heart cohort on god’s green earth!They are not. And the reason is uncomfortable but simple: we have built a formidable arsenal for treating heart disease, while doing far too little to prevent the conditions that cause it. Chronic stress, sedentary work, diets filled with refined carbohydrates and trans fats, disrupted sleep, unchecked hypertension, and a genetic predisposition to insulin resistance are working on Indian bodies every single day, largely unopposed.A precision genetic test is of little use to a patient who then returns to sixteen-hour workdays and a plate of fried food eaten in a rush. And that too swallowed down in a distracted fashion with little or no chewing. Here is what forty years in operating theatres has taught me: the most powerful cardiac intervention I know is not a stent or a bypass graft. It is years, even decades, before either becomes necessary. And this is precisely where India now has an extraordinary, almost unrepeatable opportunity.We are, right now, building the health-tech and insurance infrastructure that could make India a global leader in cardiac prevention rather than a global leader in cardiac disease. Wearable devices that track heart rate variability and sleep quality are becoming affordable. Early imaging techniques (coronary calcium scoring, carotid intima-media thickness) can now detect atherosclerosis building silently, years before any chest pain occurs. Insurance companies are beginning to link premiums to preventive health metrics. Telemedicine reaches towns that many generations of surgeons never visited.The opportunity before us is to fuse these two strands: high technology and lifestyle medicine, into a single, coherent strategy, rather than treating them as separate worlds. A young executive should not merely receive a genetic risk score; she should receive, in the same visit, a concrete plan for sleep, movement, and stress management, tracked and reinforced by the very wearable on her wrist. A corporate wellness program should not stop at an annual health check-up; it should use that data to intervene before the heart attack, not annotate the file afterward.I have spent my career repairing the damage of delayed preventive measures. It would make me happy to spend the next decade doing less repair and more prevention. Not because cardiology has failed, but because it finally succeeded upstream in every home, where it matters the most.India has the tools. What remains is the will to use them before the operating table becomes necessary, not after. The gap between 282 and 233 is not a mystery. It is a choice we have not yet fully made.Dr Ramakanta Panda, World’s leading cardiac surgeon and Chairman, Asian Heart Institute, MumbaiGet the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: The fitness trap: Why healthy-looking people are having heart attacks
articles.summary: We hear it almost every day now. Someone who looks young, fit, and active suddenly collapses out of nowhere.
articles.body: We hear it almost every day now. Someone who looks young, fit, and active suddenly collapses out of nowhere. News stories like this make everyone pause and wonder how a sudden heart crisis can happen to people who seem completely healthy.For World Heart Day, we sat down for a simple chat with Dr Ashok Seth, Chairman of Fortis Escorts Heart Institute, New Delhi, and a renowned heart expert. Instead of using heavy medical terms, he explained in simple words how everyone can protect their heart.Here are the key heart-care tips he shared, from daily habits to expert advice:1. Don't ignore the hidden warning signs in your bodyConditions like high blood pressure, diabetes, and rising cholesterol do not send loud warning signals in the beginning - they develop silently. Getting routine blood tests done is essential for everyone, especially if heart issues run in your family.2. Re-think your fitness goalsWorking out hard at the gym and building heavy muscles do not automatically mean your heart is safe. Instead of overexerting yourself with intense lifting, balance your routine with heart-friendly cardio like a 40-minute brisk walk, swimming, or cycling.3. Clean up your daily diet and habitsStay away from fast food, pastries, and fried street food like samosas and pakoras, which are packed with bad fats. Use healthy cooking oils like mustard, olive, or sunflower oil instead. Also, avoid smoking and passive smoking (secondhand smoking), which can raise your heart attack risk by 30%.4. Manage daily stress and city pollutionCity pollution and everyday mental stress take a heavy toll on your arteries. Try adding yoga or meditation to your daily routine to help keep your mind calm and balanced.5. Never stop your prescribed medicines on your ownIf a doctor puts you on cholesterol-lowering medication, make sure to keep taking it. Stopping it on your own will only cause your bad cholesterol levels to jump right back up.6. Know what to do in the first 30 minutes of an emergencyDo not brush off chest discomfort or sweating as mere gas. Avoid taking random emergency pills like sorbitrate, which can drop your blood pressure dangerously, and always get to a hospital right away.Taking care of your heart does not have to be complicated. It all starts with small, daily habits and paying attention to your body.Want to know the essential blood cholesterol and preventive screenings every man and woman should get, why even the fittest gym-goers get trapped, and the hidden everyday habits that put silent pressure on your heart?Find out the answers to all this and more - watch the full podcast to catch the entire conversation!Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in the story are independent professional judgments of the doctors/experts, and TIL does not take any responsibility for the accuracy of their views. articles.title: 4 simple habits can help slow muscle loss as you age, fitness expert says
articles.summary: A fitness coach reveals four key strategies to slow age-related muscle loss, from daily protein intake to strength training and sleep habits.
articles.body: As Americans increasingly turn to GLP-1 medications — which have been linked to a loss of lean muscle, especially during rapid weight loss — experts say preserving strength and mobility should be a priority as people age. Jacob Zemer, a New York-based fitness coach who primarily trains clients ranging from 35 to 55 years old, said that beyond GLP-1s, there are several other reasons that adults start losing muscle as they get older. "The biggest change is lifestyle," he told Fox News Digital. "When you're in your teen years or your 20s, you're running around, you're doing activities that lend themselves to building muscle." FITNESS EXPERT REVEALS 6 THINGS PEOPLE OVER 35 SHOULD DO AFTER WORKOUTS TO STAY STRONG That tends to change as people shift focus to career and family, the expert said. "You simply become more sedentary, which lowers your metabolism and your level of activity, so you're going to have less muscle." As people approach their 40s, hormone levels begin to change for both men and women, Zemer noted. "That means we partition the calories we're using less and less for protein and building muscle, and more and more for simply storing as fat," he said. THIS EXERCISE HABIT MAY SLASH DEMENTIA RISK AND HELP YOU LIVE LONGER, STUDY FINDS "We see this all the time … people start to store fat in their tummies, and they start have less muscle." Zemer said he believes that everyone should be "very mindful" about building muscle, starting from a young age. "All the way up into your 50s, your goal should be to build muscle so that when you enter your golden years — your 60s, 70s, 80s — it's kind of like your 401K," he said. "You're going to be depleting from it as you go through life. So in your 30s and 40s, you just have to be more strategic about it, because your lifestyle has changed. You need to go to the gym and train in order to have that muscle later in life." Zemer shared the following strategies that can help people slow down muscle loss as they age. No. 1: Get adequate protein Protein helps to stimulate muscle protein synthesis, the body's process of repairing and building muscle, according to Zemer. EATING TOO MUCH PROTEIN COULD BACKFIRE, EXPERTS WARN AFTER LONGEVITY REVIEW Including enough protein in your daily diet can help reduce the risk of sarcopenia, which is the age-related loss of muscle mass and strength. While people’s protein needs will vary based on age, activity level and fitness goals, Zemer said people who regularly strength-train generally benefit from higher intake. "If you're a sedentary person, you don't need to be obsessed with protein," he told Fox News Digital. "Very few people aren't getting enough protein in terms of macronutrients. But if you're training and going to the gym, you want to be getting somewhere between 0.8 to 1 gram of protein per pound of body weight." No. 2: Strength-train regularly For general health, the U.S. Physical Activity Guidelines recommend that adults strength train at least two days per week, working all major muscle groups (legs, hips, back, abdomen, chest, shoulders and arms). The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention advises using moderate or greater intensity until it's difficult to complete another repetition with good form. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES The guidelines also recommend pairing the strength training with 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity (or 75–150 minutes of vigorous activity) each week. Lifting weights isn’t just about building muscle, but also preserving muscle, according to Zemer. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "Even if you have a busy week, and you went to the gym and you lifted weights 30 minutes twice a week, that may not be enough to build new muscle, but that is certainly enough to maintain muscle," he said. "So it's very important that you lift weights a couple of times a week as you age." For beginners, Zemer recommends focusing on a few basic functional movements. Body-weight exercises like squats, lunges, push-ups and pulling movements help build strength for everyday activities, while carrying weighted objects — known as a farmer's carry, Zemer said — can improve grip, balance and overall stability. For people who feel intimidated by the gym, working with a qualified trainer for a few sessions can help boost confidence and refine technique, according to Zemer. No. 3: Get sufficient sleep Perhaps the most difficult strategy for maintaining muscle is to get enough quality sleep — seven to nine hours, Zemer emphasized. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Now, if you don't get that every night, you're not going to lose muscle," he noted. "But when you start to look at actual serious sleep deficiency, like we're talking five hours consistently, that is when you see rapid muscle loss." No. 4: Find alternatives if necessary "The worst thing you can do, even if you're injured, is to stop doing anything," Zemer said. "Find things you can do. Even if something hurts you, even if your knees aren't like what they used to be." Even without structured workouts, regular movement can help slow age-related muscle loss, while being sedentary is associated with rapid declines in muscle mass and strength, the expert cautioned. GLP-1s and muscle loss The above strategies are especially important for people who are taking GLP-1 medications for weight loss, Zemer noted, as these drugs can lead to muscle loss in the absence of strength training or adequate protein. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "If you are on a GLP-1, just remember you're accelerating the rate of fat loss, but you're also accelerating the rate of lean muscle," he said. "You want to make sure you're getting that protein and training, so that you are not losing muscle on top of the fat loss."

articles.title: An Orthopedic Surgeon’s No. 1 Test of Balance and Mobility for Healthy Aging
articles.summary: Dr. Jocelyn Wittstein, an orthopedic surgeon, reveals the at-home test you can do to maintain your mobility and work on your balance as you age.
articles.body: Changes to the ways we move is a typical sign of aging. Physical strength changes, the way we walk might look different and we’ll likely notice a difference in our balance, too, according to the National Institute on Aging. Slowing those changes and working to maintain mobility is critical to healthy aging. It means fewer falls, a reduced likelihood of disability and the chance to continue aging independently. In fact, aging adults who preserved their mobility were less likely to develop disease and end up hospitalized, and had a better quality of life, adds the NIA. There’s one move in particular that can help to ensure your future is a mobile one. Test your balance with this expert-approved test and see how you fare. Fitness Tip of the Day: Try the Y-Balance Test to Check Your Balance and Mobility Asses your mobility, strength and balance with the Y-balance test, says Dr. Jocelyn Wittstein, an orthopedic surgeon and co-author of “The Complete Bone and Joint Health Plan.” There’s no need for any fancy equipment or special skills. Just you and your balance. Why It Matters Mobility, strength and balance, says Wittstein, are three factors “important for preventing falls, and falls prevent fractures.” The Y-balance test calls on you to challenge your lower body mobility, particularly in your hips, ankles and knees. Additionally, she says, it engages the thighs, glutes, hip muscles and the core. By keeping these body parts strong and agile, you’ll maintain bone health and your ability to live and move about on your own. Your balance will improve, too, reducing your likelihood of falling, which is the leading cause of injury in those 65 years old and above, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. How to Get Started Start by standing on your left leg, says Wittstein. Elevate and extend your right leg in front of you. Reach it forward as far as you can. Then, swing that same leg behind you and extend it at an angle to your right. After that, swing it behind your standing leg to extend it at an angle to your left. You will have drawn a “Y” with your foot. Then, return to your standing position and repeat on the other side. “If that’s too difficult, you can do this with a smaller movement,” says Wittstein. Instead of keeping your right leg elevated, tap your toe to the ground as you make the “Y” formation with your legs. Simplify the Y-balance test even more by extending your right leg to tap it in front of you before returning to a standing position. Then tap it at the first angle behind you and return to standing position. Then tap it a final time while crossing your right leg behind your left and return to standing position. TODAY’s Expert Tip of the Day series is all about simple strategies to make life a little easier. Every Monday through Friday, different qualified experts share their best advice on diet, fitness, heart health, mental wellness and more.

articles.title: Simone Biles Addresses Recent Health Issues, Opens Up About Eczema Journey
articles.summary: Simone Biles talks with TODAY.com about her recent health issues, including the two inflammatory skin conditions she was diagnosed with this year.
articles.body: After surviving a health scare Simone Biles described as “almost dying” a few months ago, she’s in a much better place. Biles declined to go into detail, but tells TODAY.com that she’s “a lot better” these days. “Obviously, (I have) trusted professionals around me and great, great doctors, so I’m doing a lot better,” she explains. “It’s still an interesting road, but I am doing a lot better.” And that’s not the only health issue the 7-time Olympic gold medal gymnast has been dealing with. A little over two years ago, Biles noticed itchy, flaky red patches of skin on her scalp and skin. “I was really self-conscious of it at first, so I kind of brushed it to the side,” she says. But as an athlete, the itchiness and flakes started to impact her in new ways, she says, recalling “standing at the chalk bucket, just itching until I’m bleeding.” In Paris for the 2024 Olympic Games, Biles started opening up about the flakes on her scalp on TikTok. “If people noticed on the TV, I didn’t want them to say something before me,” she says. “So I was like, I have to address this because you couldn’t just avoid it. If they zoomed in, you could probably see it.” After the Olympics, she got even more self-conscious about the flaking amid a flurry of on-camera appearances and photoshoots. While her hairstylist at home knew about the issue, having to explain the state of her skin and scalp to a new hair and makeup crew every time was exhausting and took a toll on her mental health. “That’s when I felt it was the worst,” she says. Biles and her hairstylist tried over-the-counter products and all kinds of oils to no avail. She happened to have a dermatologist appointment for a “dent” in her arm, she explains, and she took the opportunity to ask about her skin issues while she was there. Earlier this year, Biles was finally diagnosed with two skin conditions: eczema on her arms and seborrheic dermatitis on her scalp. ‘Cousin’ Inflammatory Conditions Seborrheic dermatitis and eczema are different conditions, but can both cause itchiness, redness and flaking skin, Dr. Angela Lamb, board-certified dermatologist, tells TODAY.com. In many cases, what most of us refer to as dandruff is actually caused by seborrheic dermatitis, Lamb explains. “We really understand it to be an inflammatory response; it’s an over-response of your body to just natural things,” she says. In particular, the condition develops as a response to malassezia, a type of harmless yeast that occurs normally on the scalp. And that response leads to the greasy patches, itchiness, redness and flaking. It’s not an infection, nor is it a sign of bad hygiene, Lamb explains, noting that misconceptions like these often prevent people from getting proper treatment. Eczema, also called atopic dermatitis, is considered a “cousin inflammatory condition” to seborrheic dermatitis, Lamb says. But eczema is typically triggered by other things in the environment, such as changes in weather or humidity, or exposure to allergens like dust mites. Although Biles once suspected her symptoms were linked to stress, she hasn’t noticed any particular pattern or cycle to her flares that point to a consistent trigger, which Lamb notes is common. For seborrheic and atopic dermatitis, triggers can be “all over the map,” Lamb explains. A Simple, Effective Routine to Prevent Flare-Ups Today, Biles keeps her skin healthy with a simple routine revolving around prescription medication: Zoryve, a drug that blocks an enzyme involved in inflammatory skin responses. She uses a foam version of the medication on her scalp and face to manage seborrheic dermatitis, and she uses a cream version on her arms to keep eczema in check. Biles is helping to launch the Skin to Believe In campaign, from the makers of Zoryve, which encourages those living with inflammatory skin conditions to talk to their doctors about their symptoms. Otherwise, Biles keeps her skin-care routine pretty minimal “in a healthy way,” she says. Biles and her sister “do as much as we need to, but we’re never overdoing it, like trying all the new masks,” she explains. And she generally steers clear of perfume to avoid irritating her skin. Cutting Through the Stigma Biles hopes that speaking openly about her skin journey helps other people understand what they’re experiencing and get the professional guidance they need rather than feeling isolated or self-conscious. “At first I was really embarrassed and ashamed,” she says. “But then once I owned it, I felt a little bit more confident because then I could tell people what I was going through and exactly what it was.” That’s even extended to her husband, Indianapolis Colts safety Jonathan Owens. Biles noticed that he has similar seborrheic dermatitis symptoms and, at first, worried that she “gave” the condition to him. But, as she learned more about it (and that it’s not contagious), Biles also helped him see that it’s nothing to be ashamed of. “Like I was in denial, he was in denial,” she says. But the same way he started therapy after seeing her go through her mental health journey, “I think I have motivated him in some form, and he’s like, ‘Okay, this is a normal thing. A lot of people have it,’” Biles says. And while taking that first step to get help might be “a little bit scary,” Biles says, once you’ve done it, you’ll look back and think, “Oh, that was easy. I don’t know why I suffered for so long.”

articles.title: ‘Superman’ star Christopher Reeve’s son reveals 'shock' cancer diagnosis at age 34
articles.summary: Will Reeve, son of Christopher Reeve, revealed his embryonal carcinoma diagnosis and orchiectomy on air, drawing parallels to his parents' battles.
articles.body: Will Reeve, son of the late famed "Superman" actor Christopher Reeve, announced that he recently battled cancer. The "Good Morning America" correspondent, 34, shared during Tuesday’s show that he was diagnosed with testicular cancer earlier this year, assuring viewers that he is "OK." "The diagnosis was a shock and the treatments were a slog," he said. "Today, though, I am relieved to announce that we arrived at our destination and this cancer is in the rearview mirror. But what a journey." WILLIAM SHATNER SAYS DOCTOR DISMISSED KEY WARNING SIGN BEFORE STAGE 4 CANCER DIAGNOSIS Reeve said he found a "hard, tender lump in [his] left testicle" just a few months after his wedding to luxury event planner Amanda Dubin. An ultrasound revealed that he had "a mass that had to come out." After undergoing surgery to remove the testicle (an orchiectomy), Reeve discovered the mass was embryonal carcinoma. The aggressive subtype of testicular cancer can spread more quickly than some other forms, according to the American Cancer Society. POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY PLAY SURPRISING ROLE IN CANCER OUTCOMES Reeve later underwent a second surgery to remove lymph nodes from his abdomen after some cancer cells had spread there. The surgery took place at Memorial Sloan Kettering, which is where his mother, Dana Reeve, died from lung cancer in 2006 at age 44. His father died in 2004 at the age of 52. Reeve shared that he also underwent two rounds of chemotherapy to lower the risk that the cancer would return. He said he experienced several side effects from the medication, including ringing in the ears, bone pain, night sweats, blood clots and constant headaches. He did not lose his hair because he used a method called "cold capping," which is used during certain chemotherapy treatments to help reduce hair loss by cooling the scalp and constricting blood vessels. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES After finishing his second round of chemotherapy on July 31, Reeve said he received "clean scans" on Sept. 8. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER In an interview with People, Reeve said he is "going to be fine," although it has been "one heck of a chapter." "I’m fortunate that I caught this early," he said. "Yes, I had to jump through some flaming hoops to get to the other side, but it could have been much worse had I ignored it or delayed going to the doctor." Reeve also praised his wife for serving as his "caregiver," similar to how his mother helped care for his father after a 1995 horseback-riding accident left him paralyzed. "I learn[ed] more about what it was like to be my dad in the final nine years of his life, where he had my mom and our family taking care of him," Reeve said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He added that the experience taught him how to "repurpose [adversity] into something hopeful." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Testicular cancer is among the most treatable cancers, particularly when detected early, according to the American Cancer Society. Experts recommend seeing a doctor promptly for any lump, swelling, pain or change in a testicle. Fox News Digital reached out to Reeve’s representatives requesting comment.

articles.title: 9 Best Fruits to Help Reduce Blood Pressure, Cholesterol and Heart Disease Risk
articles.summary: Fruit reduces heart disease risk by lowering cholesterol, blood pressure and inflammation. Cardiologist recommends eating berries, apples,  watermelon and more.
articles.body: Fruit is a friend to the heart, boosting its health by lowering some of the key risk factors for cardiovascular disease. Eating plenty of fruits may play a “major role” in preventing clogged arteries, which can lead to a heart attack, studies have found. The soluble fiber in fruit can improve cholesterol, for example, says Dr. Annapoorna Kini, a cardiologist at the Mount Sinai Fuster Heart Hospital in New York. “The American diet has very little fiber. The usual fiber recommendation is more than 20 grams, 25 to 30 is ideal, but nobody can get that,” Kini tells TODAY.com. Soluble fiber dissolves in water and forms a gel-like substance in the gut, which traps cholesterol and its precursors. It’s then excreted in a bowel movement, naturally lowering cholesterol levels in the body. Eating lots of whole fruits may also reduce the risk of developing high blood pressure, researchers reported in the journal Hypertension. Fruits contain potassium, which can help ease tension on blood vessel walls and reduce the effects of too much sodium, the American Heart Association notes. Then, there’s fruit’s power to reduce inflammation — thanks to its vitamins and antioxidants — which may reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease, according to the National Heart, Lung and Blood Institute. It’s best to eat a variety of whole fruits to get lots of different nutrients, and consume fruit fresh, rather than cooking or baking it, to avoid losing any of the nutrients in the process, Kini says. She also advises avoiding fruit juice, which can lead to a “sugar rush” since it’s missing the fiber of whole fruit. Here are nine fruits to consider when aiming to reduce heart disease risk: Berries “You should try to eat some fruits with the best fiber, so berries probably are the best,” Kini says, adding, “Raspberry has the highest fiber.” Anthocyanins, the plant pigments that give blueberries their signature color, can improve endothelial function, or blood flow, studies note. Eating blueberries daily lowered systolic blood pressure, the top number of the reading. A higher intake of anthocyanins, which are also found in strawberries and blackberries, was associated with a 32% reduction in the risk of a heart attack, a study found. Berries are among cardiologists’ favorite fruits. Grapes Grapes contain phytonutrients — beneficial compounds produced by plants such as resveratrol, which has been studied for its cardioprotective benefits. These compounds are mostly found in the skin of the fruit, says registered dietitian Natalie Rizzo, nutrition editor for TODAY. Grape polyphenols, a subgroup of phytonutrients, can lower blood pressure, researchers noted, identifying grapes as fruits that have shown “potent cardiovascular protective action.” Others on the list include blueberries, pomegranates, apples and avocado. Apples The popular fruit is rich in pectin, a soluble fiber. Eating two apples a day was shown to lower cholesterol and improve cardiometabolic biomarkers in a randomized trial. Quercetin, a flavonoid in apples, can decrease systolic blood pressure by three points, research has found. Flavonoids are plant compounds with health benefits, and quercetin possesses “strong anti-inflammatory capacities,” studies note. Don’t peel your apples: The skin contains most of the fruit’s fiber and quercetin, Rizzo advises. Pears Apples and pears are similar when it comes to nutrient content, but pears have even more fiber. One medium pear has 6 grams of fiber, or about 20% of the daily recommended amount, Rizzo notes. “This delicious fruit is my secret weapon for meeting your fiber goals,” she says. Pear or apple intake “significantly decreased” the risk of cardiovascular death, a review of studies found. Avocado An abundance of research links avocados with heart health, Rizzo points out. It has good fat and is a tasty butter substitute. Registered dietitian Kristin Kirkpatrick lists avocados on her list of foods that lower blood pressure. A review of studies found eating avocados twice a day as part of a low saturated fat and cholesterol diet can help lower total and LDL cholesterol, the type that clogs arteries. A separate study found higher avocado intake was associated with lower risk of heart disease. Citrus Fruits Flavonoids found in oranges, lemons and grapefruit can reduce inflammation, cholesterol and blood pressure, a potential reason why they have a “therapeutic role” against atherosclerosis and cardiovascular disease, a study notes. The membranes and pith of citrus fruits contain pectin, a soluble fiber. Pomegranate These fruits contain brilliantly red arils, or seeds, that are high in antioxidants. The color comes from anthocyanins, the beneficial plant pigments also found in blueberries. Pomegranate juice can “significantly decrease” both the top and bottom number of the blood pressure reading, a review of studies found. A compound produced in the body after eating pomegranates improves the heart’s ability to relax, which could lead to treatment that may help some heart failure patients, researchers at King’s College London reported in August. Watermelon “Anything that is red color is good because red color contains a thing called lycopene. This lycopene is a good antioxidant,” Kini says. “Watermelon has a lot a lot of lycopene.” The amount of lycopene in watermelon is about 40% higher than raw tomatoes, the American Heart Association notes. Watermelon is also rich in citrulline, an amino acid linked to the production of nitric oxide, which is important for blood vessel health, the AHA adds. Cherries Eating cherries has “significant potential” to reduce the risk factors associated with cardiovascular disease, a study notes. Like berries, these deeply hued fruits are “rich sources of bioactive compounds” and contain flavonoids and anthocyanins that can help reduce blood pressure and cholesterol.

articles.title: Lady A’s Charles Kelley Reveals Rare Blood Cancer Diagnosis After ‘Random’ Health Concern Sparked Testing
articles.summary: Lady A’s Charles Kelley has revealed that he has been diagnosed with a “rare” blood cancer.
articles.body: Lady A’s Charles Kelley has revealed that he has been diagnosed with a “rare” blood cancer. The 45-year-old shared the health news in a video posted on his Instagram Sept. 29. As he spoke, his wife, Cassie Kelley, sat by his side and linked arms with him. “Hey, everybody! Just wanted to give a quick update on some health issues I’m dealing with, I had this couple random rib fractures that happened, which sparked you know my doctor into having me do several different blood tests,” he explained. Kelley continued: “And one of the last blood tests we did, they found a blood cancer in there called multiple myeloma, and it’s rare.” He said he is maintaining a hopeful outlook following the diagnosis. He noted that he is healthy, young and that there have been advancements in cancer treatments. The musician also shared that he has a friend who is going through the same health journey. “I think in the same spirit of the way we’ve kind of shared a lot of my sobriety journey, just getting this stuff off your chest is so freeing, and it takes the power away from it a little bit. That we wanted to let y’all know what was going on, but we’re going to get through it,” he added. He shared that through his sobriety he has learned he has to take life one day at a time and let go of control. So, he is focusing on feeling great and on the upcoming release of Lady A’s next album. The band has a group of shows scheduled around the holidays, as well. “You know, this first six months of treatment I believe is not going to be too super invasive. I can still work. I think physically, I will feel like myself. I’ll have tough days, but, you know, I want to keep working,” he said. Kelley told his fans he will keep them updated about his health journey. “It’s just another hurdle, and you know, I feel confident that we’re going to get through it,” he said before the video message ended. Fans filled the comments with stories about their similar health struggles. Kelley also received support from celebrity friends. Martina McBride said, “Love you! Here for whatever you need. You got this!” Brittney Spencer commented, “Sending so much love as yall journey through this.” Jake Owen wrote, “Love you guys .. praying for all yall and lifting you up brother.” Multiple myeloma is a cancer of the blood that starts in the plasma cells and builds up in the bone marrow, according to the Mayo Clinic. The condition can increase the risk of fractures, as Kelley experienced, because it causes the bones to become weaker, according to the International Myeloma Foundation. Cassie Kelley re-shared her husband’s message on her Instagram story and uploaded two more videos. She said she was on her way to an event to raise money for St. Jude’s Children’s Research Hospital and “honestly nothing feels more appropriate than that today.” She became emotional as expressed her gratitude for all the kind messages the couple has received during a “really hard season.” As she wiped away tears, she added that her husband’s sobriety taught her “stuff really heals in community. So that’s why we wanted to share this news.” “This is just a season for us,” she concluded. As both Kelley and his wife mentioned, he has spoken candidly over the years about becoming sober. When he appeared on TODAY in 2023 with Lady A, he opened up about having to postpone one of the band’s tours so he could prioritize his health. “I lived one way for so long and now I’m finding so much more purpose. I’m connecting to my spirituality like I never have before,” he told Hoda Kotb. “It just got really old and exhausting the last few years. It wasn’t fun anymore, really. I’m just loving this kind of new lease on life.”

articles.title: Dengue fever outbreak triggers states of emergency in 3 southern counties
articles.summary: Three Florida counties declared emergencies as 190 locally acquired dengue fever cases were confirmed, with Hillsborough County reporting 170 infections.
articles.body: Three Florida counties have declared states of emergency amid the spread of dengue fever in the state. As of Sept. 23, Pasco County, Hillsborough County and Pinellas County have made the declarations due to a spread of the mosquito-borne disease, according to each county’s news release. The local emergency declarations allow county officials to expedite mosquito-control operations, make emergency purchases, coordinate response efforts and, where applicable, seek state or federal assistance or reimbursement, the releases state. TROPICAL DISEASE SPREAD BY MOSQUITOES CLAIMS FIRST RECORDED DEATH IN SOUTHERN US STATE Under Florida law, local emergency declarations expire after seven days unless they are renewed. A total of 190 locally acquired dengue cases have been confirmed across six Florida counties, according to the latest Florida Department of Health surveillance report, which covered cases with onset through Sept. 19. Of the 190 locally acquired cases, 170 were reported in Hillsborough County, seven each in Miami-Dade and Pinellas counties, three in Orange County, two in Pasco County and one in Palm Beach County. The 190 locally acquired infections are separate from travel-associated dengue cases reported in Florida this year. TICK-BORNE 'RABBIT FEVER' SPREADS WITH CASES REPORTED NEAR MAJOR METRO AREA Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral illness that can cause fever, severe aches, nausea, rash and, in rare cases, life-threatening complications, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. "The Aedes mosquitoes that can transmit dengue are active during the day and thrive in warm, humid environments like those found in Florida." Dengue is endemic in many tropical and subtropical regions, including Southeast Asia, the Western Pacific islands, Latin America and Africa. Though less common in the continental U.S., locally acquired cases have been recorded in Florida, California and Texas. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "The Aedes mosquitoes that can transmit dengue are active during the day and thrive in warm, humid environments like those found in Florida," an entomologist spokesperson at the SC Johnson Center for Insect Science and Family Health, makers of OFF!, said in a statement sent to Fox News Digital. "As dengue cases continue to be reported in the Tampa area, taking steps to help prevent mosquito bites is especially important," the expert went on. "Staying aware of local mosquito activity and consistently protecting against bites are important steps people can take to help reduce their risk." Stopping the spread The Florida Mosquito Control Association (FMCA) previously said crews are increasing aerial and ground treatments in areas showing dengue virus activity, while also inspecting private properties for potential mosquito breeding sites, according to reports. FMCA has urged residents to empty or cover standing water around their homes. The mosquito that spreads dengue is a container breeder, meaning it lays eggs in buckets, planters, plant saucers, tires, discarded toys and other objects that collect small amounts of water, experts say. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER The SC Johnson Center for Insect Science and Family Health entomologist shared the following recommendations to prevent the spread of mosquito-borne disease. The FMCA also advises people to dress in long sleeves, light colors and closed-toed shoes outdoors. Symptoms and treatment Many people infected with dengue have no symptoms, and most people who do become sick recover within a week or two, according to Mayo Clinic. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ In some cases, however, the illness can progress to severe dengue, a potentially life-threatening condition. Symptoms typically begin four to 10 days after the bite of an infected mosquito. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Warning signs can develop quickly, often within a day or two after the fever subsides. Those may include severe stomach pain, repeated vomiting, unusual bleeding or bruising, difficulty breathing, extreme tiredness and irritability, or restlessness. People experiencing warning signs of severe dengue should seek immediate medical care.

articles.title: Bruce Willis Shares Sweet Moment With His Daughter in Rare Photo
articles.summary: Tallulah Willis, daughter of Bruce Willis, shared a photo of her father online. It’s a rare glimpse into the actor’s life following his dementia diagnosis.
articles.body: In a rare social media occurrence, Tallulah Willis shared a photo of her father on her Instagram account. The Sept. 28 post features Tallulah Willis, 32, the actor’s youngest daughter with Demi Moore, planting a kiss on her father’s head. The caption reads, “so cute! 😚😚” The “Die Hard” star was diagnosed with frontotemporal dementia, or FTD, in 2023, after first being diagnosed with aphasia in March 2022 and stepping away from acting. The regressive disease mainly affects communication and behavior, rather than memory, like more common forms of dementia. Tallulah Willis has been previously vocal about her dad’s condition. His early symptoms, she wrote in a 2023 essay, “started out with a kind of vague unresponsiveness.” Fearing he’d become preoccupied with his two youngest daughters he had with second wife, Emma Heming Willis, following his divorce from Moore, “I thought he’d lost interest in me.” She soon realized, after a series of cognitive tests, that his behavioral changes were linked to something else entirely. Once her father was diagnosed, Tallulah Willis took it upon herself to savor the moments she shares with him. “I find that I’m trying to document, to build a record for the day when he isn’t there to remind me of him and of us,” she wrote. While his demeanor and language capabilities have changed, their connection continues to run deep, Tallulah writing that her father still “lights up when I enter the room.” In June, 2025, Tallulah Willis shared another glimpse into her family’s life with an Instagram post she captioned, “Sunday Funday at Grams !” In the series of photos, Tallulah holds her father’s hand in one and hugs him in another. In them, Bruce Willis smiles. Though his life has taken a turn, the former actor isn’t aware of his diagnosis, Heming Willis revealed. “He never connected the dots that he had this disease. I’m really happy about that. I’m really happy he doesn’t know about it,” she said during a podcast appearance. Bruce Willis remains surrounded by his five daughters, his granddaughter, ex-wife, Moore, and Heming Willis. Moore and Willis remain close after being married from 1987 to 2000, with the actress continuing to share sweet photos of their family together, including Heming Willis, Bruce Willis’ full-time caregiver.

articles.title: People with Type 2 diabetes lost up to 60 pounds on Lilly’s latest weight loss drug
articles.summary: Eli Lilly’s highly anticipated GLP-1 drug retatrutide helped people with Type 2 diabetes lose up to 60 pounds, or about 23% of their body weight, according to late-stage trial results published Tuesday in The Lancet.
articles.body: Eli Lilly’s highly anticipated GLP-1 drug retatrutide helped people with Type 2 diabetes lose up to 60 pounds, or about 23% of their body weight, according to late-stage trial results published Tuesday in The Lancet. It’s the most weight loss ever recorded in a drug trial for diabetes patients, a group that often has a harder time losing weight. In clinical trials for semaglutide and tirzepatide, people with Type 2 diabetes lost up to 10% (21 pounds) and 15% (34 pounds) of their body weight, respectively. (Those are not direct comparisons, as the drugs were not evaluated in head-to-head clinical trials.) Retatrutide “is truly an advance in diabetes care,” said Dr. Susan Spratt, an endocrinologist and the senior medical director for the Population Health Management Office at Duke Health in North Carolina. She was not involved in the trial and does not receive money from Eli Lilly. “It rivals gastric bypass surgery without the surgery.” Spratt said many diabetes medications, such as insulin, cause weight gain. “It can be discouraging to manage your diabetes well but gain weight,” she said. Lilly’s trial included more than 1,110 patients who had an average starting weight of about 234 pounds and an average body mass index, or BMI, of about 38. People were randomly assigned to take one of three weekly doses of retatrutide or a placebo for 80 weeks. By the end of the trial, more than half of participants’ BMI fell below 30, the cutoff for obesity. Results from another trial, published Tuesday in the New England Journal of Medicine, found retatrutide helped patients without Type 2 diabetes who have obesity or are overweight lose up to 70 pounds, or 25% of their body weight on average, after 80 weeks. That data included a subset of patients with severe obesity, who lost up to 85 pounds, or 30% of their body weight, after 104 weeks — the most weight loss ever recorded in a medication trial and on par with bariatric surgery. Like semaglutide and tirzepatide, retatrutide works by mimicking a hormone called GLP-1. What sets retatrutide apart is its classification as a “triple agonist.” Lilly’s tirzepatide, a “double agonist,” mimics two hormones (GLP-1 and GIP), and retatrutide targets three by adding a hormone called glucagon. Lilly hasn’t submitted retatrutide for approval with the Food and Drug Administration, but its clinical trial results have already cemented it as one of the drug industry’s most highly anticipated treatments. Lilly says it plans to file for approval early next year. Unauthorized, copycat versions of retatrutide are already being made and sold through wellness platforms, med spas and compounding pharmacies. The drug is often labeled as “for research use only,” a legal workaround to sell compounds they claim aren’t meant for humans. Lilly has filed lawsuits against companies selling unapproved versions of the drug. Retatrutide’s other benefits Retatrutide also helps reduce the severity of sleep apnea and lower knee arthritis pain. Earlier data suggests the drug appears to help the heart. The new trial found that retatrutide, like other GLP-1 drugs, which were initially developed as diabetes medications, effectively lowered blood sugar levels in patients with diabetes. Retatrutide lowered A1C levels — a measure of a person’s average blood sugar levels over the previous two to three months — by up to 1.6%, compared with 0.2% with a placebo, according to the trial results. Up to 40% of patients in the trial reached an A1C below 5.7%, below the cutoff for diabetes and prediabetes. “The retatrutide data is very exciting,” Dr. Michelle Ponder, an assistant professor of medicine at Duke University School of Medicine in North Carolina, wrote in an email. A 5.7% A1C level means “that their diabetes went into remission,” said Ponder, who was not involved with Lilly’s trial. She added, however, that retatrutide “may be too strong for some patients,” particularly those with only mild diabetes or slightly elevated weight. They “may be better suited to the medications we already have available on the market such as Ozempic or Mounjaro,” she said. She added that whenever switching medications, there is a chance patients could experience a change in the frequency of side effects. Side effects of retatrutide were similar to other GLP-1 medications, with patients most commonly reporting diarrhea, nausea, constipation and vomiting. Lilly said the side effects were mild to moderate in severity. About 8% of people in the trial taking the highest dose stopped taking the drug, compared with about 5% of people taking the placebo.

articles.title: 'Mum sent them £140,000': How to spot the signs a loved one is being scammed
articles.summary: Helen discovered her mum was in the grip of a romance scam - here's how she found out and broke her free.
articles.body:
Head over heels in love with a man she met online, Helen's mother hollowed out a book and put £10,000 cash inside. She then posted it to a Shanghai Hospital where he awaited a life-saving operation.

Once he was better they would be together - but the demands kept coming. Then a new man came on the scene - he'd been kidnapped and if she didn't pay the ransom he would be killed.

In total she sent £140,000 to romance scammers.

The first time Helen knew something was wrong was when her mum accidentally sent messages intended for the criminals to her. Then she became more secretive.

"It became obvious to me something was going on again," she says.

Here's how to spot the signs a loved one is being scammed and how to help them.

Helen's 80-year-old mum met her scammers on Facebook where they used artificial intelligence (AI) to change their appearance in photos and video calls - a type of deception known as deepfake .

With criminals employing increasingly sophisticated tactics, cases of fraud in the UK are on the rise. Over £1.3bn was stolen by scammers in 2025.

Helen noticed her mum taking a lot of phone and video calls but would not say who she was speaking to. Helen says she felt "emotionally drained" trying to work out what was happening.

"I didn't feel like I could cope with not having any tool to deal with it," she tells BBC Radio 4's Scam Secrets . "That's not expertise that most families have got."

Scam Secrets presenter Shari Vahl says these are the signs to look out for:

Shopping in unusual ways such as buying gift cards

Unusual financial activities like bank transfers and opening new accounts

Communicating online or by the phone in a way that's out of character

Families should be 'curious but not confrontational'

In a bid to get her mum to open up, Helen decided "to try and be calm about this and open up the possibility she could trust me".

Dale Richardson, a police fraud protect officer, encourages families to be "curious but not confrontational".

"I like to break it down... and listen to them and say, right, how did you meet? And what have they said?"

Helen convinced her mum to allow her to speak to the scammer on a video call.

She says she quickly spotted the deepfake as the image was "fuzzy" and his voice out of sync with his movements.

Helen tried to convince her mum the man she was speaking to was not who he said he was but she did not believe her.

"She was saying I made her feel disgusted and ashamed," says Helen. "And that I should let her have her relationship and not intervene."

Forensic linguist Dr Lis Carter, who is part of the Scam Secrets team, stresses the importance of being patient and careful with your words when trying to help loved ones who believe they are in a genuine relationship.

"Being a family member coming into that, you are 'destroying' that happiness."

Unable to break her mum away from the scam, Helen turned to her bank.

She had a lasting power of attorney, meaning she could act on behalf of her mum and set up safeguards for her accounts.

Jim Winters, head of economic crime at Nationwide, says anyone who believes a family member is being scammed should contact their bank.

"They might be limited in what they can share with you for data privacy reasons, but they can take steps to safeguard that account," he says.

"Once we know that a customer is being defrauded we can spot the hallmarks very quickly and take steps to break that spell."

To date, the bank that Helen's mum uses has returned £45,000 to her account.

Though Helen changed her mum's phone number three times, she continued to give the new one to the scammers.

Helen eventually replaced her mum's smartphone with one that could only do calls and texts.

Winters also advises "completely resetting" a loved ones digital footprint by changing telephone numbers, email address and social media accounts.

"That's what makes you visible, that's what puts you out there. So taking steps to reset all of that is so important," he says.

Ask open questions - be calm and patient to gather information

Contact their bank - they can put safeguards in place

Enlist someone impartial - this can help victims open up

Reset their digital footprint - scammers can't continue if they can't contact them
